pos: n. (spirit, breath, the soul; rendering Hebrew gava' in the idiom, Greek pneuma)
etymology: From Saxon gast, spirit or breath, cognate with German Geist. In the Authorized Version it means spirit, never an apparition of the dead. Hence the two great uses: the Holy Ghost, the third Person of the Trinity, and to give up the ghost, to breathe out one's spirit in death.
biblical_def: Ghost in the Authorized Version means spirit, and carries none of the modern sense of a haunting. Its first use is of death: “Then Abraham gave up the ghost, and died in a good old age, an old man, and full of years” (Genesis 25:8) — the spirit surrendered, not extinguished, and the man gathered to his people. Mark uses the same idiom of the crucifixion, and places the centurion's confession immediately after it: “when the centurion... saw that he so cried out, and gave up the ghost, he said, Truly this man was the Son of God” (Mark 15:39). Its greater use is of the third Person of the Trinity. The Holy Ghost overshadows Mary at the incarnation (Luke 1:35); He is the one lied to by Ananias, whom Peter identifies in the next breath as God (Acts 5:3-4); He is named with the Father and the Son in the baptismal formula (Matthew 28:19); He makes overseers in the church (Acts 20:28); and by Him the love of God is shed abroad in the hearts of believers (Romans 5:5).
webster_summary: Spirit or breath; in the Authorized Version never an apparition. Used of the human spirit surrendered in death — gave up the ghost — and above all of the Holy Ghost, the third Person of the Godhead.
webster_full: GHOST, n. [Sax. gast, spirit, breath; Ger. Geist.] Spirit; the soul of man.
2. To give up the ghost, to die; to yield up the spirit.
3. The Holy Ghost, the third person in the adorable Trinity.
4. In later usage, the soul of a deceased person appearing to the living; a sense not found in the common version.
5. In Scripture, Abraham gave up the ghost, Gen. 25; baptized with the Holy Ghost, Acts 11.
corruption_summary: The Holy Ghost is diminished in two directions: reduced to an impersonal force or influence, as by the Jehovah's Witnesses and much popular speech, or detached from the word and made the warrant for whatever a movement wishes to do.
corruption_paragraphs: That the Spirit is a Person and is God is not an inference but a plain statement of the text. Peter tells Ananias he has lied to the Holy Ghost and immediately says thou hast not lied unto men, but unto God. He is named alongside the Father and the Son in one baptismal name, singular. He speaks, forbids, is grieved, distributes gifts as He wills, and searches the deep things of God — none of which an influence can do. The Nicene faith, which the dictionary holds without reservation, confesses Him as the Lord and Giver of life, proceeding from the Father and the Son, who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified.

The opposite error keeps the Person and severs Him from Scripture. Where the Spirit is claimed as the source of new revelations, of ecstatic practice, or of directives that Scripture does not contain, He is invoked against His own work; He is the Author of the written word, and He does not contradict Himself. The dictionary's position is cessationist: the canon is closed, and the Spirit's present work is to illuminate what He has already given, to regenerate, to convict, to sanctify, and to seal. That is not a lesser ministry than the one claimed for Him by movements that need signs; it is the greater one.
roots_summary: Hebrew ruach is breath, wind, and spirit; the idiom for dying is gava', to expire. Greek pneuma covers the same range, and ekpneo is to breathe out, used of Christ's death.
roots_lines: Hebrew ruach (H7307) — breath, wind, spirit; used of the Spirit of God moving upon the face of the waters.
Hebrew gava' (H1478) — to expire, to breathe out; the verb behind gave up the ghost.
Greek pneuma (G4151) — breath, wind, spirit; the New Testament word for both the human spirit and the Holy Ghost.
Greek ekpneo (G1606) — to breathe out, to expire; used of Christ giving up the ghost in Mark 15:37.
Saxon gast — spirit, breath; cognate with German Geist, the root of the English word.
usage: Of a patriarch's death at a full age: Then Abraham gave up the ghost, and died in a good old age (Genesis 25:8).
Of the Spirit at the incarnation: The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee (Luke 1:35).
Of the Spirit appointing overseers in the church: over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers (Acts 20:28).
scriptures: Genesis 25:8
Then Abraham gave up the ghost, and died in a good old age, an old man, and full of years; and was gathered to his people.
Luke 1:35

And the angel answered and said unto her, The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God.
Acts 5:3
But Peter said, Ananias, why hath Satan filled thine heart to lie to the Holy Ghost, and to keep back part of the price of the land?
Acts 20:28
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.

pos: n. (one near at hand; rendering Hebrew rea', Greek plesion)
etymology: From Saxon neahgebur — neah, nigh, and gebur, a dweller: one who dwells near. The Authorized Version keeps the British spelling. Hebrew rea' means a companion, friend, or fellow, and is wider than mere proximity.
biblical_def: Neighbour is the one near at hand, and he is the subject of the whole second table of the law. Four of the Ten Commandments name him directly or by implication, including the ninth: “Neither shalt thou bear false witness against thy neighbour” (Deuteronomy 5:20). The summary of that table is the command Christ set second only to the love of God: Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. When a lawyer sought to narrow the field — “willing to justify himself, said unto Jesus, And who is my neighbour?” (Luke 10:29) — the Lord answered with the parable of the good Samaritan and reversed the question, asking not who qualifies as my neighbour but to whom I proved neighbour. Proverbs fills in the ordinary duties: do not defer a good you can do today (“Say not unto thy neighbour, Go, and come again, and to morrow I will give; when thou hast it by thee”, Proverbs 3:28), and do not wear out a welcome (Proverbs 25:17). Ezekiel names the defilement of a neighbour's wife among the sins that forfeit the land.
webster_summary: One who dwells near; and in Scripture, any person with whom one has to do. He is the subject of the second table of the law — thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself — and the lawyer's attempt to narrow the term was answered by the good Samaritan.
webster_full: NEIGHBOUR, n. [Sax. neahgebur; neah, nigh, and gebur, a dweller.] One who lives near another.
2. One who is entitled to, or who receives, kind treatment from another; a fellow being.
3. An intimate; a confidant; one with whom one has dealings.
4. NEIGHBOUR, v.t. To adjoin; to border on; to be near to.
5. In Scripture, thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself, Lev. 19; And who is my neighbour? Luke 10.
corruption_summary: The lawyer's question — asked to justify himself — is still the standard evasion: define the neighbour narrowly enough and the commandment costs nothing. Christ answers by refusing the definition and pointing to the man who acted.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke tells us the motive plainly: the lawyer was willing to justify himself. A definition of neighbour that excluded most people would have left him already obedient, and that is what he was fishing for. The parable frustrates it twice over. The neighbour who acts is a Samaritan, a man the lawyer would have excluded from the category; and the ones who pass by are a priest and a Levite, men whose vocation should have compelled them. Christ then rephrases the question — which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbour unto him that fell among the thieves? — turning it from who deserves my love into whom I am able to help.

The commandment is also abused in the other direction, by an undifferentiated benevolence that discharges itself on distant causes while neglecting those actually near. Scripture orders the duties: a man who provides not for his own house has denied the faith, and Paul instructs the church to do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith. Proverbs 3:28 gives the practical test, and it is uncomfortably concrete — do not tell a neighbour to come back tomorrow for what you have in the house today. The neighbour in Scripture is a particular person with a name, not humanity in the abstract.
roots_summary: Hebrew rea' means a fellow, friend, or companion, and is the word in the second great commandment; shaken is the dweller nearby. Greek plesion is literally the one near, and ho plesion is the neighbour of the commandment.
roots_lines: Hebrew rea' (H7453) — a friend, companion, fellow; the word in love thy neighbour as thyself.
Hebrew shaken (H7934) — an inhabitant, one dwelling nearby; neighbour in the local sense.
Greek plesion (G4139) — near, close by; with the article, the neighbour of the commandment.
Greek agapao (G25) — to love with deliberate goodwill; the verb governing the neighbour in Matthew 22:39.
Saxon neahgebur — a nigh-dweller; the compound behind the English word.
usage: Of the ninth commandment: Neither shalt thou bear false witness against thy neighbour (Deuteronomy 5:20).
Of an attempt to narrow the commandment: willing to justify himself... And who is my neighbour? (Luke 10:29).
Of good not to be deferred: Say not unto thy neighbour, Go, and come again (Proverbs 3:28).
scriptures: Deuteronomy 5:20
Neither shalt thou bear false witness against thy neighbour.
Luke 10:29
But he, willing to justify himself, said unto Jesus, And who is my neighbour?
Proverbs 3:28
Say not unto thy neighbour, Go, and come again, and to morrow I will give; when thou hast it by thee.
Proverbs 25:17
Withdraw thy foot from thy neighbour's house; lest he be weary of thee, and so hate thee.

pos: n. pl. (cattle used for draught and sacrifice; rendering Hebrew baqar and shor, Greek bous)
etymology: The old plural of ox, from Saxon oxa, plural oxan — one of the very few English nouns that still forms its plural in -en, with children and brethren. In Scripture oxen are the chief draught animal, a principal measure of wealth, and a costly sacrifice.
biblical_def: Oxen are the working cattle of Scripture, and they appear at three points of biblical life. They measure wealth: Pharaoh enriched Abram for Sarai's sake, and “he had sheep, and oxen, and he asses, and menservants, and maidservants, and she asses, and camels” (Genesis 12:16) — a list that is also a record of Abram's failure of nerve. They are offered in sacrifice at the sealing of the covenant at Sinai, where young men “sacrificed peace offerings of oxen unto the LORD” (Exodus 24:5), and by Balak in his attempt to purchase a curse (Numbers 22:40). They carry the molten sea in Solomon's temple, twelve of them, three toward each quarter of the earth (1 Kings 7:44). And Proverbs uses them for one of the most practical sentences in the book: “Where no oxen are, the crib is clean: but much increase is by the strength of the ox” (Proverbs 14:4) — a clean stable means an empty barn, and productivity always comes with mess.
webster_summary: The plural of ox; the working cattle of Scripture, used for ploughing and treading out grain, counted as wealth, and offered in sacrifice. Proverbs makes them the figure for productive work: where no oxen are, the crib is clean.
webster_full: OXEN, n. pl. [Sax. oxa, pl. oxan.] The plural of ox; cattle of the bovine kind, used for draught and for food.
2. In Scripture, a chief measure of a man's substance, reckoned with sheep, asses and camels.
3. An animal of sacrifice; the bullock of the burnt offering and the peace offering.
4. It is one of the few English nouns retaining the old plural in en, with children and brethren.
5. In Scripture, sacrificed peace offerings of oxen unto the LORD, Exo. 24; much increase is by the strength of the ox, Prov. 14.
corruption_summary: Proverbs 14:4 is a standing rebuke to a tidiness that mistakes the absence of mess for good order. Fruitfulness has costs — in a stable, in a household, in a church — and the clean crib is often the sign of nothing happening.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is that productive life is untidy. A barn with no oxen needs no mucking out, and it also produces no harvest; the proverb sets the two facts side by side and leaves the reader to choose. The application is wide. A household with children is noisier and more expensive than one without; a church that receives sinners will have problems a closed club never faces; a ministry that attempts anything will make errors that a dormant one avoids. In each case the cost is the evidence of life.

The proverb does not commend carelessness, and Scripture elsewhere requires that all things be done decently and in order. The point is the direction of the tradeoff. Where the avoidance of trouble becomes the governing aim, the result is not holiness but sterility — the servant who buried his talent had a spotless record and was called wicked and slothful. The same law of the ox appears in Paul's hands twice, when he applies thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn to the support of ministers: the working animal is to eat of the work it does.
roots_summary: Hebrew baqar is the collective for cattle or herd, and shor is a single head of ox; 'eleph is also used of oxen. Greek bous is the ox, and tauros the bull of sacrifice.
roots_lines: Hebrew baqar (H1241) — cattle, herd, oxen; the collective noun for the bovine stock of a household.
Hebrew shor (H7794) — an ox or bullock, singly; the animal of the goring-ox laws in Exodus 21.
Hebrew 'ebus (H18) — a crib or manger; the clean crib of Proverbs 14:4.
Greek bous (G1016) — an ox; the animal Paul names in the muzzling law applied to ministers.
Greek tauros (G5022) — a bull; the sacrificial animal named in Hebrews 10:4.
usage: Of wealth reckoned in livestock: he had sheep, and oxen, and he asses, and menservants (Genesis 12:16).
Of the sacrifices at the sealing of the covenant: sacrificed peace offerings of oxen unto the LORD (Exodus 24:5).
Of productivity and its costs: Where no oxen are, the crib is clean (Proverbs 14:4).
scriptures: Genesis 12:16
And he entreated Abram well for her sake: and he had sheep, and oxen, and he asses, and menservants, and maidservants, and she asses, and camels.
Exodus 24:5
And he sent young men of the children of Israel, which offered burnt offerings, and sacrificed peace offerings of oxen unto the LORD.
1 Kings 7:44
And one sea, and twelve oxen under the sea;
Proverbs 14:4
Where no oxen are, the crib is clean: but much increase is by the strength of the ox.

pos: n. pl. (married women; rendering Hebrew nashim, Greek gunaikes)
etymology: The plural of wife, from Saxon wif, a woman. The plural is theologically significant in Scripture because its very existence in a household marks a departure from the creation ordinance of Genesis 2:24, which joins one man to one woman.
biblical_def: Wives is the plural of wife, and Scripture's handling of the plural is one of the clearest cases of its method: it records without commending. The first man to take more than one wife is a murderer in the line of Cain — “Lamech took unto him two wives: the name of the one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah” (Genesis 4:19) — and the boast of vengeance he sings to them follows immediately. Thereafter polygamy attends the patriarchs, the judges, and the kings, and in every single case Scripture reports the resulting misery: rivalry between Sarah and Hagar, between Leah and Rachel, between Hannah and Peninnah; and Solomon's wives turning away his heart. Benjamin's tribe is nearly extinguished and the elders must contrive “How shall we do for wives for them that remain” (Judges 21:16) at the end of a book whose refrain is that every man did what was right in his own eyes. Ezra's reform confronts the taking of strange wives (Ezra 10:44). Against all of it stands the creation ordinance and the qualification of an elder: the husband of one wife.
webster_summary: The plural of wife. Scripture records polygamy among patriarchs, judges, and kings without ever commending it, and attaches misery to every instance; the standard is the creation ordinance of one man and one woman.
webster_full: WIVES, n. pl. [Sax. wif.] The plural of wife; women joined to men in marriage.
2. In the plural applied to one household, it denotes the practice of polygamy.
3. Strange wives, in the Scriptures, women of the nations forbidden to Israel in marriage.
4. WIFE, n. A woman united to a man in the lawful bonds of wedlock.
5. In Scripture, Lamech took unto him two wives, Gen. 4; All these had taken strange wives, Ezra 10.
corruption_summary: Scripture's record of polygamy is used both to accuse it of endorsing the practice and, more recently, to argue that marriage has no fixed form at all. Both readings ignore that the Bible narrates these households and then shows what happened in them.
corruption_paragraphs: The pattern is unbroken and cannot be accidental. Lamech, the first polygamist, is a boastful killer. Abraham's second union produces Ishmael and a household division that outlasts him. Jacob's four wives produce a family so poisoned by favouritism that ten brothers sell the eleventh. Elkanah's two wives produce the provocation that drives Hannah to the temple in bitterness. Solomon's wives turn away his heart, and the kingdom is torn in two in his son's reign. Deuteronomy had explicitly forbidden the king to multiply wives. Scripture reports these households the way it reports David's adultery — fully, and with the consequences attached.

Christ settles the question by going behind the whole history to the beginning: from the beginning it was not so, and He quotes Genesis 2:24 — they twain shall be one flesh, not three or four. The apostolic requirement for elder and deacon is the husband of one wife. The dictionary therefore holds marriage to be one man and one woman covenanting before God for life, the only category of legitimate sexual union, and treats every departure — ancient polygamy, modern serial divorce, and the redefinitions of our own day — as a departure from a creational form that was never the church's to alter.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'ishshah means both woman and wife, its plural nashim; tsarah, a rival wife, is literally a vexer. Greek gune likewise covers woman and wife, and mias gunaikos andra is the elder's qualification.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'ishshah (H802) — a woman or wife; its plural nashim is the word rendered wives.
Hebrew tsarah (H6869) — a rival wife, an adversary; literally a vexer, as Peninnah was to Hannah.
Hebrew nokriyyah (H5237) — a foreign or strange woman; the wives put away in Ezra's reform.
Greek gune (G1135) — a woman or wife; the plural in the household codes of the epistles.
Greek mias gunaikos andra (G1520, G1135, G435) — the husband of one wife; the qualification for elder and deacon.
usage: Of the first polygamist, in the line of Cain: Lamech took unto him two wives (Genesis 4:19).
Of a tribe nearly extinguished and the expedient devised: How shall we do for wives for them that remain (Judges 21:16).
Of the reform under Ezra: All these had taken strange wives (Ezra 10:44).
scriptures: Genesis 4:19
And Lamech took unto him two wives: the name of the one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah.
Genesis 2:24
Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.
1 Timothy 3:2
A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach;
Ezra 10:44
All these had taken strange wives: and some of them had wives by whom they had children.

pos: n. and v. (a servant; to serve; rendering Hebrew sharath, Greek diakoneo and diakonos)
etymology: From Latin minister, a servant or attendant, built on minus, less — the opposite of magister, a master, built on magis, more. The word means an underling, and every ecclesiastical dignity attached to it since has been at war with its etymology.
biblical_def: Minister means a servant, and it is used in Scripture of three distinct services. It is used of a personal attendant: “Moses rose up, and his minister Joshua” (Exodus 24:13), and of the synagogue attendant who took the scroll back from Christ at Nazareth (Luke 4:20) — a functionary handling a book, in the most consequential reading in history. It is used of sacred service: the Levite “shall minister in the name of the LORD his God” (Deuteronomy 18:7), and Hezekiah charges the priests that the LORD has chosen them “to stand before him, to serve him, and that ye should minister unto him” (2 Chronicles 29:11). And strikingly, Paul applies the word to the civil magistrate, twice in one verse: “he is the minister of God to thee for good... for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil” (Romans 13:4). The word is also used of what ordinary speech can do: talk that is good to the use of edifying “may minister grace unto the hearers” (Ephesians 4:29).
webster_summary: A servant or attendant, and the verb to serve. In Scripture it covers the personal attendant, the Levite in sacred service, the civil magistrate as God's minister for good, and the speech that ministers grace to those who hear it.
webster_full: MINISTER, n. [L. minister, from minus, less; opposed to magister, from magis, more.] A servant; one who attends and serves another.
2. One to whom a sovereign or a state entrusts the direction of affairs; a magistrate.
3. One who serves at the altar; one charged with the cure of souls; a pastor.
4. MINISTER, v.i. To attend and serve; to supply things needful; as, to minister to the sick.
5. In Scripture, his minister Joshua, Exo. 24; he is the minister of God to thee for good, Rom. 13.
corruption_summary: A word that means underling has been made a title of rank. Christ founded the office on service and set Himself as the pattern, and every clerical system that reverses this — whether by vestment, by hierarchy, or by celebrity — has inverted the word it uses.
corruption_paragraphs: The Lord's teaching is explicit and is given precisely because the disciples were disputing about rank: ye know that the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them... but it shall not be so among you: but whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister. He then grounds it in His own coming — not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give His life a ransom for many. The Roman hierarchy, with its graded orders culminating in a papal monarchy, is the most developed contradiction of this, and the Reformation named it as such; but Protestant celebrity is the same sin in modern dress, and its practitioners are usually the last to see it.

The remedy is not a false humility about the office, which is genuinely honourable. Scripture says the elder who rules well is worthy of double honour, and requires that the congregation esteem such men very highly in love for their work's sake. What it does not permit is dominion — Peter, who might have claimed it, charges elders to feed the flock not as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock. Two offices, elder and deacon; a plurality of elders; and a word for both that means servant.
roots_summary: Hebrew sharath is to minister or attend, used of Joshua under Moses and of the Levites before the LORD; Greek diakoneo is to serve, especially at table, and diakonos gives both the general word for minister and the office of deacon.
roots_lines: Hebrew sharath (H8334) — to minister, attend, serve; used of both personal and sacred service.
Greek diakoneo (G1247) — to serve, especially to wait at table; the verb Christ applies to Himself.
Greek diakonos (G1249) — a servant or attendant; the word for the minister and for the office of deacon.
Greek leitourgos (G3011) — a public servant; used of the magistrate and of ministers of the sanctuary.
Latin minister — from minus, less; an underling, the opposite of magister, a master.
usage: Of a personal attendant to a prophet: Moses rose up, and his minister Joshua (Exodus 24:13).
Of the civil magistrate as God's servant: he is the minister of God to thee for good (Romans 13:4).
Of speech that serves those who hear it: that it may minister grace unto the hearers (Ephesians 4:29).
scriptures: Exodus 24:13
And Moses rose up, and his minister Joshua: and Moses went up into the mount of God.
Deuteronomy 18:7
Then he shall minister in the name of the LORD his God, as all his brethren the Levites do, which stand there before the LORD.
Romans 13:4

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
Ephesians 4:29
Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.

pos: v.i. (to be destroyed, to come to nothing; rendering Hebrew 'abad, Greek apollumi)
etymology: From Latin perire, to go through and so to be lost — per, through, and ire, to go. Hebrew 'abad means to be lost or to wander away before it means to be destroyed, and Greek apollumi keeps the same double sense, which is why the lost sheep and the perishing sinner share a verb.
biblical_def: Perish means to be lost or destroyed, and its range in Scripture runs from physical death to final ruin. It marks the danger of approaching a holy God carelessly: “charge the people, lest they break through unto the LORD to gaze, and many of them perish” (Exodus 19:21). Job describes his former charity by the condition of those he helped: “The blessing of him that was ready to perish came upon me” (Job 29:13). Christ speaks with grim irony of the city that kills its prophets: “it cannot be that a prophet perish out of Jerusalem” (Luke 13:33). But the word's greatest weight is in the gospel, where it names the alternative to everlasting life — that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life — and in the Lord's twice-repeated warning, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish. The same Greek verb describes the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the lost son, which is the mercy hidden inside the word: what is perishing is what the Shepherd goes out to seek.
webster_summary: To be destroyed; to come to nothing; to be lost. In Scripture it names both temporal ruin and final destruction, and stands as the alternative to everlasting life — should not perish, but have everlasting life.
webster_full: PERISH, v.i. [L. perire; per and eo, to go.] To die; to lose life in any manner; to be destroyed.
2. To come to nothing; to fail entirely; as, the hope of the wicked shall perish.
3. To be lost eternally; to be ruined in respect of the soul.
4. To decay; to waste away; as, the flower perisheth.
5. In Scripture, him that was ready to perish, Job 29; except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish, Luke 13.
corruption_summary: Perish is regularly pressed to mean annihilation — the wicked ceasing to exist — or, in the other direction, a temporary loss ending in universal restoration. Scripture teaches an eternal, conscious punishment, and holds it alongside a genuine and free offer of life.
corruption_paragraphs: Annihilationism, or conditional immortality, reads perish and destruction as cessation of being, and it has gained ground among evangelicals. But the same word describes the wineskins that perish without ceasing to exist, and the decisive texts are explicit about duration and consciousness: the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever, and they have no rest day nor night. Most decisively, the identical word aionios governs both destinies in Matthew 25:46 — everlasting punishment and life eternal — so that whatever limits the one limits the other. The dictionary holds eternal conscious punishment, as every historic Christian confession has.

The universalist reading fails at the same texts from the other side, and it also empties the offer of its urgency. The New Testament's missionary energy is unintelligible if none finally perish. Yet the doctrine is never taught coldly in Scripture: Christ weeps over the city He is about to sentence, and Paul writes of great heaviness and continual sorrow for his kinsmen. The mercy is real, and is embedded in the very verb — apollumi is the word for the lost sheep that the shepherd leaves ninety and nine to find. The Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'abad means to wander, be lost, or be destroyed; Greek apollumi carries the same double sense of losing and destroying, and its noun apoleia is perdition. Aionios governs the duration.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'abad (H6) — to wander away, to be lost, to perish; used of a straying sheep and of a ruined nation.
Greek apollumi (G622) — to destroy, to lose; the verb of John 3:16 and of the lost sheep, coin, and son.
Greek apoleia (G684) — destruction, perdition; the noun for the final ruin of the impenitent.
Greek aionios (G166) — eternal, everlasting; governing both punishment and life in Matthew 25:46.
Latin perire — to go through, to be lost; the root of the English verb.
usage: Of the danger of approaching a holy God presumptuously: lest they break through unto the LORD to gaze, and many of them perish (Exodus 19:21).
Of the destitute relieved by a righteous man: The blessing of him that was ready to perish came upon me (Job 29:13).
Of a nation that will not serve: the nation and kingdom that will not serve thee shall perish (Isaiah 60:12).
scriptures: Exodus 19:21
And the LORD said unto Moses, Go down, charge the people, lest they break through unto the LORD to gaze, and many of them perish.
The blessing of him that was ready to perish came upon me: and I caused the widow's heart to sing for joy.
Isaiah 60:12
For the nation and kingdom that will not serve thee shall perish; yea, those nations shall be utterly wasted.
Luke 13:33
Nevertheless I must walk to day, and to morrow, and the day following: for it cannot be that a prophet perish out of Jerusalem.

pos: v.t. (to occupy, to hold as owner; rendering Hebrew yarash, Greek ktaomai)
etymology: From Latin possidere, to sit upon or occupy. Hebrew yarash is stronger than the English: it means to take possession by dispossessing another, to inherit and to drive out, and both senses are usually present when Israel is told to possess the land.
biblical_def: Possess in Scripture is chiefly the language of inheritance, and specifically of Israel entering Canaan. Caleb, alone with Joshua against ten discouraging reports, states the case in one sentence: “Let us go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it” (Numbers 13:30). Moses sets the same command before a later generation, and does not minimise the odds: “Thou art to pass over Jordan this day, to go in to possess nations greater and mightier than thyself, cities great and fenced up to heaven” (Deuteronomy 9:1). The possession is granted, not earned — the land is what “the LORD thy God giveth thee to possess” (Deuteronomy 19:2) — and yet it must be entered and held. The word turns against those who claim what is not theirs: Edom says of Israel and Judah, “These two nations and these two countries shall be mine, and we will possess it; whereas the LORD was there” (Ezekiel 35:10). And Christ turns it inward in one of the shortest verses in the Gospels: “In your patience possess ye your souls” (Luke 21:19).
webster_summary: To occupy, hold, or own; and in Scripture chiefly to take possession of an inheritance by dispossessing another. The land was given by God and yet had to be entered and held, a pattern Christ turns inward: in your patience possess ye your souls.
webster_full: POSSESS, v.t. [L. possideo, to sit upon, to occupy.] To have and hold; to own; to occupy.
2. To seize; to enter and take possession of; as, to possess a land.
3. To have power over, as an evil spirit is said to possess a man.
4. To be possessed of, to have as an owner or a right.
5. In Scripture, Let us go up at once, and possess it, Num. 13; In your patience possess ye your souls, Luke 21.
corruption_summary: The conquest language of Deuteronomy is regularly lifted out of redemptive history and applied to present-day territory, politics, or personal ambition — possessing the land, taking territory. The promise was to a particular people, for a particular land, under a commission long since discharged.
corruption_paragraphs: Two habits misuse the word. The first is a triumphalist Christian rhetoric that speaks of taking cities and possessing regions as though the church held Joshua's commission; it does not, and the New Testament transfers the warfare entirely to weapons that are not carnal. The second is the prosperity teaching that reads the land promises as guarantees of material increase for the individual believer, so that possess the land becomes a formula for claiming a house or a career. The inheritance the New Testament actually names is incorruptible, undefiled, and reserved in heaven.

What does carry over is the structure of the promise, and it is instructive. The land was given by God's free grant and still had to be entered; the giving did not make the going unnecessary. Hebrews uses that generation as the warning: they failed to enter in because of unbelief, and the promise stood while they died in the wilderness. So Paul can say work out your own salvation with fear and trembling and add for it is God which worketh in you. Christ's inward application is the most searching form of it: in a chapter about wars, betrayals, and the destruction of Jerusalem, the thing His disciples are told to possess is themselves.
roots_summary: Hebrew yarash means to inherit, take possession, and dispossess — the three senses inseparable; nachalah is the inheritance itself. Greek ktaomai is to acquire or gain, the verb in Luke 21:19.
roots_lines: Hebrew yarash (H3423) — to inherit, to take possession, to dispossess; the standing verb of the conquest.
Hebrew nachalah (H5159) — an inheritance or possession; the portion allotted to each tribe.
Hebrew 'achuzzah (H272) — a holding or possession; the land held under God's ultimate title.
Greek ktaomai (G2932) — to acquire, to gain, to win; possess ye your souls in Luke 21:19.
Greek kleronomia (G2817) — an inheritance; the New Testament portion, reserved in heaven.
usage: Of faith against a discouraging majority: Let us go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able (Numbers 13:30).
Of an inheritance given and yet to be entered: which the LORD thy God giveth thee to possess it (Deuteronomy 19:2).
Of the inward possession Christ commands: In your patience possess ye your souls (Luke 21:19).
scriptures: Numbers 13:30
And Caleb stilled the people before Moses, and said, Let us go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it.
Deuteronomy 9:1
Hear, O Israel: Thou art to pass over Jordan this day, to go in to possess nations greater and mightier than thyself, cities great and fenced up to heaven,
Luke 21:19
In your patience possess ye your souls.
Ezekiel 35:10
Because thou hast said, These two nations and these two countries shall be mine, and we will possess it; whereas the LORD was there:

pos: v.t. (to ruin, to bring to nothing; rendering Hebrew shachath and shamad, Greek apollumi and kataluo)
etymology: From Latin destruere, to unbuild — de, down, and struere, to build. The word is the exact opposite of construction, and Scripture keeps the pairing: the God who destroys is the God who builds, and Jeremiah's commission names both.
biblical_def: Destroy is to unbuild, and Scripture applies it to God, to men, and to what men must not do. Abraham's intercession for Sodom opens with the question on which the doctrine of God's justice turns: “And Abraham drew near, and said, Wilt thou also destroy the righteous with the wicked?” (Genesis 18:23). The answer, worked out over six exchanges, is that the Judge of all the earth will do right, and that ten righteous would have spared the city. David refuses a destruction that lay easily within his power and would have ended his exile: “Destroy him not: for who can stretch forth his hand against the LORD'S anointed, and be guiltless?” (1 Samuel 26:9). Rabshakeh claims a divine commission for his campaign — “the LORD said unto me, Go up against this land, and destroy it” (Isaiah 36:10) — a claim that was partly true and wholly presumptuous. And Micah warns that a polluted land will itself destroy those who rest in it (Micah 2:10).
webster_summary: To unbuild; to ruin; to bring to nothing. In Scripture it frames Abraham's question whether God will destroy the righteous with the wicked, David's refusal to destroy the LORD's anointed, and the destruction that a polluted land works on those who rest in it.
webster_full: DESTROY, v.t. [L. destruo; de and struo, to build.] To demolish; to pull down; to unbuild.
2. To ruin; to bring to nought; to annihilate as to usefulness.
3. To kill; to slay; to extirpate.
4. To lay waste; to make desolate, as a country or a city.
5. In Scripture, Wilt thou also destroy the righteous with the wicked? Gen. 18; Destroy him not, 1 Sam. 26.
corruption_summary: God's acts of destruction are the standing objection to His goodness. Abraham raised the objection first and in the strongest terms, and Scripture records both his question and the answer, which is that God distinguishes the righteous and does not sweep them away with the guilty.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 18 is the pattern for every honest wrestling with divine judgment. Abraham does not suppress the question or apologise for it; he presses it six times, from fifty righteous down to ten, and he grounds it in God's own character: Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right? God does not rebuke him. The narrative that follows shows the answer executed — Lot is removed before a single spark falls, and the angel says I cannot do any thing till thou be come thither. Judgment in Scripture is discriminating, and the discrimination is often the part of the story readers skip.

The abuse in the other direction is the claim of a divine mandate for one's own destruction, and Rabshakeh is its portrait. He was not entirely wrong — Assyria was in fact the rod of God's anger — and he was nonetheless destroyed for saying so, because, as Isaiah 10 explains, he meant not so, neither did his heart think so. A man may be an instrument of judgment and be judged for how he wielded it. This is the standing warning to anyone who reads providence as endorsement, and the reason David would not lift his hand against Saul even when circumstance and counsel both urged it.
roots_summary: Hebrew shachath is to mar, spoil, or corrupt as well as to destroy; shamad is to exterminate. Greek apollumi is to destroy or lose, and kataluo is to loosen down, used of the temple and of the law.
roots_lines: Hebrew shachath (H7843) — to mar, spoil, corrupt, destroy; used of the earth corrupted before the flood.
Hebrew shamad (H8045) — to exterminate, to lay waste utterly; the strongest verb of destruction.
Greek apollumi (G622) — to destroy or to lose; the verb behind both perishing and destroying.
Greek kataluo (G2647) — to loosen down, to demolish; I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil.
Latin destruere — to unbuild; de, down, and struere, to build.
usage: Of intercession grounded in God's justice: Wilt thou also destroy the righteous with the wicked? (Genesis 18:23).
Of restraint toward an enemy in one's power: Destroy him not: for who can stretch forth his hand against the LORD'S anointed (1 Samuel 26:9).
Of a polluted land destroying those who rest in it: because it is polluted, it shall destroy you (Micah 2:10).
scriptures: Genesis 18:23
And Abraham drew near, and said, Wilt thou also destroy the righteous with the wicked?
1 Samuel 26:9
And David said to Abishai, Destroy him not: for who can stretch forth his hand against the LORD'S anointed, and be guiltless?
Isaiah 36:10
And am I now come up without the LORD against this land to destroy it? the LORD said unto me, Go up against this land, and destroy it.
Micah 2:10
Arise ye, and depart; for this is not your rest: because it is polluted, it shall destroy you, even with a sore destruction.

pos: v.t. and v.i. (to work for, to worship; rendering Hebrew 'abad, Greek latreuo and douleuo)
etymology: From Latin servire, to be a slave, from servus, a slave. Hebrew 'abad is the same word for labour and for worship, which is the key to the whole biblical doctrine: a man's service is his worship, and he will render it either to God or to an idol.
biblical_def: Serve in Hebrew and in Scripture does not divide neatly into work and worship, because 'abad is one word for both. Israel is told in advance that they will serve a foreign nation and be delivered: “that nation, whom they shall serve, will I judge: and afterward shall they come out with great substance” (Genesis 15:14). The jubilee law limits how a poor Israelite may serve his brother, “as an hired servant, and as a sojourner... unto the year of jubile” (Leviticus 25:40) — a term, not a life. The choice is put most memorably at Shechem, where Joshua refuses to let the nation drift: choose you this day whom ye will serve, and then commits his own household without waiting for the vote. When the people answer, he makes them their own witnesses: “Ye are witnesses against yourselves that ye have chosen you the LORD, to serve him” (Joshua 24:22). The alternative is named plainly: “Confounded be all they that serve graven images” (Psalm 97:7). And Zacharias names the end of redemption as service without fear (Luke 1:74).
webster_summary: To work for, obey, or worship. Hebrew uses one word for labour and worship alike, so that service is worship: a man serves either the LORD or an idol, and Joshua's choose you this day whom ye will serve assumes there is no third option.
webster_full: SERVE, v.t. [L. servio, from servus, a slave.] To work for; to attend at command; to labor for.
2. To obey and worship; as, to serve God.
3. To be subordinate or subject to; as, to serve a foreign nation.
4. To supply with food; to wait at table; as, to serve the tables.
5. In Scripture, choose you this day whom ye will serve, Josh. 24; they that serve graven images, Psa. 97.
corruption_summary: The modern division between a religious life and a working life is unknown to the Hebrew, which uses one word for both. Every man serves something; the question Joshua put is not whether but whom.
corruption_paragraphs: Joshua's speech at Shechem is often quoted for its final clause and rarely for its logic. He does not offer neutrality as an option: if it seem evil unto you to serve the LORD, choose you this day whom ye will serve — and the alternatives he lists are the gods beyond the flood and the gods of the Amorites. There is no third column for those who serve nothing. Christ says the same in a different idiom: no man can serve two masters, and the second master He names is not Satan but money. Modern secularity presents itself as the absence of worship; Scripture treats it as worship redirected.

This is why the Reformed doctrine of vocation matters so much. If 'abad covers both, then the farmer's field and the priest's altar are both places of service, and the medieval grading of lives by sacredness collapses. Paul tells slaves to do their work heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men, and adds that they serve the Lord Christ. What remains is only the question of the object. Joshua also made the congregation witnesses against themselves, which is worth remembering: a profession of service is admissible evidence, and it will be produced.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'abad means to work, to serve, and to worship, and gives 'ebed, a servant; Greek distinguishes douleuo, to serve as a bondman, from latreuo, to render religious service, the root of English idolatry.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'abad (H5647) — to work, till, serve, worship; one verb for labour and for worship alike.
Hebrew 'ebed (H5650) — a servant or slave; the title given to Moses, David, and the Messiah.
Greek douleuo (G1398) — to serve as a bondman; no man can serve two masters.
Greek latreuo (G3000) — to render religious service or worship; the second half of idolatry.
Latin servire — to be a slave, from servus; the root of the English verb.
usage: Of a foreign servitude foretold and judged: that nation, whom they shall serve, will I judge (Genesis 15:14).
Of a congregation made witness against itself: Ye are witnesses against yourselves that ye have chosen you the LORD, to serve him (Joshua 24:22).
Of the end of redemption: that we being delivered out of the hand of our enemies might serve him without fear (Luke 1:74).
scriptures: Joshua 24:15

And if it seem evil unto you to serve the LORD, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.
Joshua 24:22
And Joshua said unto the people, Ye are witnesses against yourselves that ye have chosen you the LORD, to serve him. And they said, We are witnesses.
Psalm 97:7
Confounded be all they that serve graven images, that boast themselves of idols: worship him, all ye gods.
Luke 1:74
That he would grant unto us, that we being delivered out of the hand of our enemies might serve him without fear,

pos: v.i. (to go away, to turn aside; rendering Hebrew sur, Greek apochoreo and analuo)
etymology: From Latin dis, apart, and partire, to divide — originally to separate, whence to go away. The older sense survives in the marriage vow till death us depart, which modern usage has altered to do part, obscuring the word's real meaning.
biblical_def: Depart is to go away or turn aside, and Scripture uses it for departures of very different weight. It carries one of the great messianic promises, in which a thing that will not depart is the point: “The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come” (Genesis 49:10) — the tribal rule preserved until the One to whom it belongs arrives. Jeremiah uses the same construction of the fixed ordinances of day and night as the guarantee of Israel's continuance: “If those ordinances depart from before me, saith the LORD, then the seed of Israel also shall cease” (Jeremiah 31:36). The wise father charges his son to keep his words in sight: “Let them not depart from thine eyes; keep them in the midst of thine heart” (Proverbs 4:21). And the word carries the most terrible sentence in the New Testament, spoken not to the openly wicked but to men who had prophesied and cast out devils in Christ's name: “I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity” (Matthew 7:23).
webster_summary: To go away; to turn aside; to separate from. In Scripture it carries the promise that the sceptre shall not depart from Judah, the charge that God's words not depart from before the eyes, and Christ's sentence, depart from me, ye that work iniquity.
webster_full: DEPART, v.i. [L. dis and partio, to divide.] To go from; to leave a place; to move away.
2. To desist; to leave; to abandon; as, to depart from a purpose or a rule.
3. To die; to decease; to leave this world.
4. In the older usage, to separate; as in the marriage vow, till death us depart.
5. In Scripture, The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, Gen. 49; depart from me, ye that work iniquity, Matt. 7.
corruption_summary: Matthew 7:23 is addressed to men who prophesied, cast out devils, and did many wonderful works in Christ's name, and it is the decisive answer to any assurance built on religious activity or spiritual power rather than on Christ Himself.
corruption_paragraphs: The frightening thing about the passage is the resume. These are not scoffers; they address Him as Lord, Lord, and they cite works that most churches would treat as unanswerable evidence. Christ's reply does not dispute the works. He says I never knew you — not you fell away, but I never knew you — and the ground of rejection is relational, not evidential. Spiritual power proves nothing about a man's standing; Balaam prophesied truly, Saul was among the prophets, and Judas was sent out with the twelve.

The passage is therefore the sharpest rebuke available to a ministry that measures itself by results, and to any believer who measures himself the same way. What Christ requires in the preceding verse is doing the will of His Father, and what He describes in the following parable is a house founded on rock — hearing His sayings and doing them. The 1689 Confession is careful here: assurance is founded on the divine truth of the promises, the inward evidence of the graces to which those promises are made, and the testimony of the Spirit of adoption. Not on works of power; not on a remembered decision; on Christ, evidenced by a changed life.
roots_summary: Hebrew sur is to turn aside or depart, used both of moral turning and of physical leaving; Greek apochoreo is to withdraw, and analuo, to loose from moorings, is Paul's word for departing to be with Christ.
roots_lines: Hebrew sur (H5493) — to turn aside, depart, remove; used of departing from evil and from the LORD.
Hebrew shebet (H7626) — a rod, sceptre, tribe; what shall not depart from Judah in Genesis 49:10.
Greek apochoreo (G672) — to withdraw, depart; the imperative in Matthew 7:23.
Greek analuo (G360) — to unloose, to depart as a ship from its moorings; Paul's word for dying.
Latin departire — to separate, divide apart; the root of the English verb.
usage: Of the messianic promise held until Shiloh comes: The sceptre shall not depart from Judah (Genesis 49:10).
Of God's words kept in sight: Let them not depart from thine eyes; keep them in the midst of thine heart (Proverbs 4:21).
Of the sentence on false assurance: I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity (Matthew 7:23).
scriptures: Genesis 49:10
The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come; and unto him shall the gathering of the people be.
Proverbs 4:21
Let them not depart from thine eyes; keep them in the midst of thine heart.
Matthew 7:23
And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.
Jeremiah 31:36
If those ordinances depart from before me, saith the LORD, then the seed of Israel also shall cease from being a nation before me for ever.
